opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The basic picture is that at some point, possibly fairly soon, we'll have AIs that are really quite good at doing the kind of research that people like me currently do: running ML experiments, writing code, analyzing results, maybe even coming up with research directions. If that happens, the amount of safety research labor available could go up by a huge factor very quickly. But that labor is only useful if we've set things up so it can be pointed at the right problems and so we can trust and check what comes out.

So a few things seem worth doing now. One is just figuring out which problems are bottlenecked on labor versus on ideas or on access to powerful models. Some research directions are pretty well specified: "run this family of experiments across lots of settings, measure this thing." Those are exactly the projects you'd want to hand to an automated researcher, and it's helpful to have them scoped out with clear success criteria, good infrastructure, and benchmarks already built. If you show up on the day when you have a million copies of a capable AI researcher and you don't have the codebases, eval suites and problem statements ready, you'll waste a lot of that early, possibly very short window.

A second thing is thinking about verification. The worry with handing research to AIs is that they might be bad at it in ways that are hard to notice, or in the worst case, they might be scheming and deliberately sabotaging safety work. So you want projects where outputs are checkable: where you can tell whether an experiment was actually run correctly, whether a result replicates, whether a proposed technique really works on held-out settings. Part of preparing now is designing research agendas that are robust to the possibility that the labor you're using isn't fully trustworthy. That connects closely to the control agenda we work on at Redwood: how do you get useful work out of models you're not confident are aligned?

Third, there's an organizational and cultural piece. Labs and safety teams need to actually be ready to allocate a lot of compute to automated safety research at the moment it becomes possible, rather than having all of that capacity go to capabilities. That's partly a political question inside companies, and it's worth people advocating for it in advance and having concrete plans, like "when models hit this capability level, we'll spend this much compute on these specific safety projects."

And I'd add a note of caution: I don't think we should lean on this so much that humans stop doing the foundational work now. The automated researchers will be most useful when they're extending well-understood agendas, and the conceptual groundwork for those agendas, plus the judgment about which results to believe, is something we need to build ourselves before we get there.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scoped projects and checkable outputs, but does not propose a portfolio whose collective completion would increase confidence in handing control over to AI.

r002.rationale: It recommends scoping projects, building infrastructure and benchmarks, and preparing compute plans before capable AI researchers arrive, warning that the early window may be short.

r003.rationale: It says to do foundational work now because automated researchers will be most useful when extending established agendas, and warns that waiting could waste a short window.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because I think it's actually one of the more important strategic questions for people doing safety research right now. The basic picture is: at some point, probably not that far off, we're going to have AI systems that can do a large fraction of the intellectual labor involved in AI safety research. And the question is, what should humans be doing now to make that go well?

I think there are a few different framings people use, and I want to distinguish them. One framing is "we should just do the research now, because the research is useful." That's fine, and I don't want to dismiss it. But another framing, which I think is underrated, is "we should be doing the work that makes it possible to hand off research to AIs later." And those can come apart quite a bit.

So what does the second thing look like concretely? A few things.

The first is just getting really clear on what the problems are. Like, a lot of the hardest part of safety research right now is not the execution, it's figuring out what question you're even asking. If you have a bunch of AIs that are very good at running experiments, writing code, doing math, but you can't tell them precisely what you want, you're going to waste a lot of that capability. So I think there's real value in people doing the kind of conceptual clarification work where, at the end, you have a problem statement that's crisp enough that you could plausibly hand it to a very competent but not especially wise collaborator and expect them to make progress.

The second thing is building the evaluation infrastructure. If an AI does a bunch of safety research for you, how do you know whether it's good? This is actually a pretty hard problem. In a lot of science, you have a nice external check: the experiment works or it doesn't, the theorem is proven or it isn't. In safety research, a lot of the outputs are things like "here's an argument that this technique is robust" or "here's a proposed protocol," and checking those requires taste and judgment. And if we're worried that the AIs doing the work might be subtly misaligned or just subtly wrong, then our ability to check becomes the bottleneck. So I think building better ways to evaluate research outputs, things like having clearer success criteria, having benchmarks, having ways to adversarially test proposals, is really valuable preparation.

The third thing, which is more in the vein of what I work on, is thinking about the control side of this. If you're going to have AIs doing your safety research, you want to be in a position where even if those AIs are trying to mislead you, you're not totally hosed. That means you want research processes where there are checks, where you can audit outputs, where you have some redundancy. And figuring out what those processes look like before you need them seems a lot better than improvising once the models are already capable enough to be dangerous.

I'll also say there's a somewhat uncomfortable implication here, which is that some research that seems valuable now might be less valuable than it looks, because it's the kind of thing that'll be cheap to do later with AI help. If something is basically "run a thousand experiments and see what happens," I'm somewhat less excited about a human spending two years on that right now, versus someone figuring out which thousand experiments we should run and how we'd interpret the results. Not that the execution work is worthless, you often learn a lot by doing it, and you need the empirical grounding to have good taste. But the relative value shifts.

The flip side, and I want to be honest about this, is that it's really easy to use "preparing for AI-assisted research" as a rationalization for not doing anything concrete. There's a failure mode where you spend all your time on meta-level planning and never produce anything. I think the way to avoid that is to actually try doing the handoff at whatever level current models allow. Like, try to get current models to do pieces of your research. See where they fail. That tells you a lot about what the bottlenecks are going to be, and it keeps you grounded in what's actually hard versus what you imagine is hard.

So my overall take is something like: the humans in the loop should be increasingly focused on problem specification, evaluation, and the overall structure of the research process, and should be actively practicing delegation now so that when the models get good enough, the transition is smooth rather than chaotic. And we should be doing this with the explicit awareness that the models we're delegating to might not be fully trustworthy, so the processes need to be robust to that.

r001.rationale: The response recommends clarifying problems and preparing research handoffs, but does not propose a portfolio of projects whose collective completion would increase confidence in handing control to AI.

r002.rationale: It recommends preparing for AI-assisted research now—by clarifying problems, building evaluation methods, and practicing delegation—before models become capable enough to do much of the research.

r003.rationale: It says control processes should be worked out before powerful models are needed and dangerous, but does not argue that lead times in AI control research justify starting that work now rather than waiting for AI to make it easier.

astra-6.text:
I think one useful thing to do now is to get projects to the point where we know what we’d ask an AI to do, and how we’d tell whether it had succeeded. That’s often a lot of the hard part. “Do some good safety research” is a much less useful assignment than “Here’s a particular phenomenon we want to understand, here’s an experimental setup, and here are some measurements that would help us distinguish between these hypotheses.”

So you might want to build the infrastructure, try a few experiments, and understand where the difficulties are, even if you don’t expect to finish the project with the resources you currently have. You’re trying to put yourself in a position where a large increase in available research labor actually translates into progress.

There’s an important complication, though, which is that the AI helping you with safety research might itself be untrustworthy. So I’d be particularly excited about projects where we can check the outputs fairly well, rather than projects where success means the AI writes an extremely persuasive argument that its own deployment would be safe.

And I wouldn’t want to take this all the way to waiting around for better models. Doing research now is part of how you learn which questions are useful and which evaluations actually tell you anything. The preparation should involve enough real work that you’re finding out where your plan is wrong.

r001.rationale: The response recommends making individual projects actionable, but does not propose a portfolio whose collective completion would increase confidence in handing control over to AI.

r002.rationale: It recommends doing preparatory work now so projects can make progress when AI systems provide substantially more research labor later.

r003.rationale: It argues against waiting for better models, but does not cite lead times in AI control research as the reason to start now.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a pretty useful distinction between doing safety research now and setting things up so that future AI systems can do safety research effectively. Those overlap, but they’re not quite the same thing.

Suppose you expect that in a few years you’ll have access to AIs that are very good programmers and can run experiments much faster than your current team. Then one thing you can do now is identify questions where the bottleneck will be doing a lot of implementation and experimentation, and get those questions into a sufficiently clear form. What’s the experiment? What would count as success? How would you tell whether the result actually supports the conclusion you care about?

The last part seems particularly important. It’s much easier to delegate work if you can evaluate the output. If you ask an AI to ‘solve alignment’, you have this enormous problem of figuring out whether it did. If you ask it to implement a particular experiment, where you understand how to check the implementation and interpret the results, that’s a much more manageable situation.

So I’d want a portfolio of projects that are ready to hand off, along with the infrastructure and evaluation methods to make the results useful. And I’d practise delegating pieces of those projects to the systems we have now. That helps you discover where your instructions are underspecified, or where you were relying on a researcher having judgment that you don’t know how to check.

I wouldn’t want to assume that future AIs will be trustworthy just because they’re useful at research. Part of preparing is figuring out how to get valuable work out of them while keeping the parts we can’t verify from becoming the foundation of our safety argument.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a portfolio of projects ready to hand off, but does not say that completing them would increase confidence in handing control over to AI.

r002.rationale: It recommends preparing clear research questions, experiments, and evaluation methods now so future, more capable AIs can carry out the work.

r003.rationale: The response says to prepare before more capable AIs arrive, but does not argue that lead times in AI control research justify starting work now.
